name: Sulfur (topical)

angle.text: Topical sulfur is an old over-the-counter option in masks, soaps and spot treatments for acne, rosacea and body breakouts, popular among people avoiding harsher actives. Rosacea has decent trial support; the acne data are thinner.

summary: Old-school OTC sulfur for acne and rosacea: long in use, with decent rosacea trial support and thinner acne data.
note: Acne-specific controlled data are limited; the strongest support is for rosacea (with sodium sulfacetamide) and scabies.
currentQuick:
Topical sulfur is a long-established ingredient in acne washes, masks and spot treatments, and is also used for rosacea, seborrhoeic dermatitis and scabies.
Dermatology reviews list sulfur/sodium sulfacetamide among rosacea therapies backed by multiple randomised trials. For acne specifically, the available sources include a label and a comedogenicity study but few controlled efficacy trials.
How it works: Sulfur is generally described as keratolytic and antimicrobial, though the reviewed sources give little mechanistic detail.
Risks and caveats: OTC acne products carry external-use-only warnings. A randomised study found no link between sulfur and comedone formation under its conditions. Trials in scabies and hand eczema did not highlight prominent adverse effects in their abstracts.
deepLead:
Topical sulfur is one of the oldest dermatological treatments, used in lotions, creams, soaps, masks and spot treatments for acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea and scabies. It is sold over the counter in the United States in products labelled for acne.
For appearance purposes it is used mainly for acne. Dermatology reviews describe topical sulfur combined with sodium sulfacetamide as one of the rosacea therapies validated by more than one randomised controlled trial, and randomised trials have also tested sulfur in scabies and hand eczema. Trial evidence for sulfur as a standalone acne treatment is thinner in the sources reviewed, and registered acne studies involving sulfur combinations are of unknown status.

name: Topical finasteride

angle.text: Topical finasteride is applied to the scalp to slow pattern hair loss while limiting systemic exposure and side effects, and is used by people who want to keep their hairline. Trials are encouraging but smaller than for the oral drug.

summary: Scalp-applied finasteride aimed at cutting systemic DHT and side effects; trial data are encouraging but smaller than for the oral drug.
note: Reviews describe real but variable systemic DHT reduction; the oral drug carries documented sexual and mood adverse-event reports.
currentQuick:
Topical finasteride puts the hair-loss drug finasteride on the scalp as a spray, solution or gel instead of a daily pill, often mixed with minoxidil. The goal is to keep hair benefits while reducing whole-body exposure.
Small randomised trials, a phase III spray trial and a systematic review report hair-count gains, and one meta-analysis found no significant efficacy difference from oral finasteride. Evidence is smaller and less standardised than for the oral drug.
How it works: Finasteride blocks type II 5-alpha-reductase, which converts testosterone to DHT, a hormone linked to scalp follicle miniaturisation. Applied topically, it lowers scalp DHT; studies also report some drop in plasma DHT.
Risks and caveats: Oral finasteride is associated with sexual side effects and a depression warning in the US label, and persistent symptoms are discussed as post-finasteride syndrome. Topical use was designed to reduce systemic exposure but still lowers plasma DHT in studies. It is prescription-only or off-label in most settings, and concentrations and formulations vary.
deepLead:
Topical finasteride is finasteride, a type II 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, formulated for application to the scalp rather than taken as a daily tablet. It is used off-label or as a compounded or newer branded preparation for androgenetic alopecia (male and female pattern hair loss), with the stated aim of reducing the drug's systemic exposure and thereby its side effects.
A 2018 systematic review of seven human studies reported that topical finasteride decreased the rate of hair loss and increased hair counts, with reductions in both scalp and plasma dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and no change in serum testosterone, while describing the evidence as preliminary. A 2022 review with meta-analysis concluded that topical 1 percent finasteride solution was not significantly different in efficacy from oral 5 mg and 1 mg doses. A phase III randomised trial of a topical finasteride spray has been published, with further phase III work in Chinese men.
In a 2025 Delphi-based Canadian consensus, topical finasteride was among seven interventions recommended for androgenetic alopecia. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to keep finasteride's hair benefit while avoiding oral side effects; users disagree on how much it lowers serum DHT.

name: Fluridil

angle.text: Fluridil, sold in Europe as Eucapil, is a topical antiandrogen used for pattern hair loss by people seeking a non-systemic option. Evidence is a single small 2002 trial.

summary: Obscure topical antiandrogen (Eucapil) for hair loss, backed by a single small 2002 trial.
note: Only one small randomised trial is known; it was reported by its developers and has not been independently replicated in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Fluridil is a topical antiandrogen sold in Europe as Eucapil for androgenetic alopecia. It is meant to block androgen receptors locally in the scalp rather than lowering hormones throughout the body.
The published evidence is a single 2002 randomised trial in 43 men, which reported a rise in anagen-phase hair percentage over placebo and no changes in sexual function or lab values.
How it works: Fluridil is described by its developers as suppressing the human androgen receptor while being highly hydrophobic, easily degraded by hydrolysis and not absorbed into the body.
Risks and caveats: The 2002 study found no irritation or sensitisation in patch tests and normal sexual function and blood values, but it was small and short, and long-term data are not available. It is not an approved drug in the US.
deepLead:
Fluridil (marketed in Europe under the name Eucapil) is a topical antiandrogen developed for androgenetic alopecia. Its authors describe it as a novel agent that suppresses the human androgen receptor locally in the scalp, is highly hydrophobic and breaks down by hydrolysis, and is not absorbed systemically.
The published clinical evidence is a single early study: a 2002 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 43 men with androgenetic alopecia, reported alongside a patch-test safety study in 20 men. The trial reported an increase in the proportion of hairs in the anagen (growth) phase, and no changes in sexual function, libido, blood counts or blood chemistry. No larger or independent trials appear in the sources reviewed.

name: Caffeine shampoo

angle.text: Caffeine shampoos such as Alpecin are marketed to people with thinning hair as an easy addition to a hair-loss routine. Evidence is one trial in women, with little else behind it.

summary: Marketed anti-hair-loss shampoo (Alpecin and others); one women's trial exists, with little else behind it.
note: Evidence in the sources reviewed is a single study in women; results were not available.
currentQuick:
Caffeine shampoos are cosmetic products sold to slow thinning hair, with Alpecin the best-known brand. They are used as a scalp wash rather than a drug.
The only study found examined a phyto-caffeine shampoo in women with female androgenetic alopecia; its results were not available, and no men-specific trial was found.
How it works: Marketing and study background describe caffeine as promising in vitro and in vivo for androgenetic alopecia; the sources reviewed do not detail the proposed mechanism.
Risks and caveats: No safety information was available in the sources reviewed. These are sold as cosmetic products rather than approved hair-loss drugs.
deepLead:
Caffeine shampoo refers to cosmetic shampoos containing caffeine, marketed for people with thinning hair; the best-known brand is Alpecin. The idea is that caffeine applied to the scalp may counter the effects of androgens on hair follicles.
Evidence for these products in the sources reviewed is limited to a single study: a cosmetic phyto-caffeine shampoo evaluated in women with female androgenetic alopecia, published in 2020 in the Giornale Italiano di Dermatologia e Venereologia. Its abstract says caffeine-based products have shown promise in vitro and in vivo, but the results of the study are not available in the excerpt reviewed.

name: Tongkat ali

angle.text: Tongkat ali is a root extract sold as a natural testosterone booster, taken in pursuit of better muscle, leaner body composition and libido. Small trials lean positive on testosterone and mood, while broader reviews are more sceptical.

summary: Southeast Asian root extract sold as a 'natural test booster'; small trials lean positive, but broader reviews are sceptical.
note: Trials are small and results differ between reviews; one study found it altered propranolol bioavailability.
currentQuick:
Tongkat ali is a Southeast Asian root used traditionally as an aphrodisiac and now sold as a testosterone-support supplement. It is popular in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles.
A 2022 meta-analysis of small randomised trials found higher total testosterone with E. longifolia, especially in men with low levels, but a 2024 review of 27 testosterone boosters concluded most do not raise total testosterone, and erectile-function results are mixed.
How it works: Lab and rat studies suggest its quassinoids act on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and on steroidogenic enzymes; forum posts also claim it lowers SHBG, which the sources reviewed do not confirm.
Risks and caveats: Safety data are limited; a 2010 review noted gaps in safety evidence for commercial products, and one study found a water extract changed propranolol absorption. It is sold as a supplement, so product content varies.
deepLead:
Tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia, also called longjack or Malaysian ginseng) is a Southeast Asian shrub whose root is used in traditional medicine as an aphrodisiac and for fever, and is now sold worldwide as a dietary supplement marketed as a natural testosterone booster. The roots contain quassinoids and alkaloids such as eurycomanone.
In human research, a 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials found that E. longifolia supplementation was associated with higher serum total testosterone, with the authors noting a stronger effect in hypogonadal and aging men. A 2024 systematic review of 27 proposed testosterone boosters concluded that most do not raise total testosterone against placebo, and counted E. longifolia among the agents assessed with three studies. A meta-analysis of two randomised trials found no significant overall improvement in erectile function.
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it is discussed as a legal, low-risk supplement for testosterone, libido and training; members disagree on how large any effect is compared with testosterone replacement or anabolic steroids.

name: Fadogia agrestis

angle.text: Fadogia agrestis is a podcast-popular stem extract taken, often stacked with tongkat ali, as a testosterone booster for muscle and libido. Support comes from rat studies; human trials are lacking.

summary: Podcast-famous African stem extract sold as a testosterone booster; supported only by rat studies, with toxicity questions unanswered in humans.
note: No human trials; rat studies include testicular and liver/kidney toxicity work, and supplement content varies.
currentQuick:
Fadogia agrestis is an African plant whose stem extract is sold as a testosterone and libido supplement, usually alongside tongkat ali. It became widely known through podcasts and fitness social media.
Almost all evidence is from rats, including a 2005 study reporting higher serum testosterone and more mating behaviour. No human clinical trial was found.
How it works: In rodents, extracts raised serum testosterone and, in a rat erectile model, shifted nitric oxide pathway markers; the mechanism in humans has not been studied.
Risks and caveats: Rat studies have looked at testicular function and liver and kidney toxicity, and related plant species cause cardiac toxicity in livestock. Human safety data do not exist, and a 2019 analysis found supplement contents differ widely.
deepLead:
Fadogia agrestis (now often classified as Vangueria agrestis) is a plant of the coffee family, Rubiaceae, native to tropical Africa. Its stem has been used in traditional African medicine as an aphrodisiac and for pain and inflammation, and extracts are sold as dietary supplements marketed for testosterone and libido.
The research is almost entirely in rodents. A 2005 study in male rats reported higher serum testosterone and more sexual behaviour after dosing with an aqueous stem extract, and a 2023 rat study reported effects on erectile-dysfunction biomarkers. Rat studies have also examined testicular function and liver and kidney toxicity. No human clinical trial of Fadogia agrestis was found in the sources reviewed.
In forums and on podcasts it is often combined with tongkat ali in 'natural testosterone' stacks, and the combination is discussed alongside concerns drawn from the animal toxicity studies.

name: Shilajit

angle.text: Shilajit is a Himalayan mineral resin taken for testosterone, energy and recovery, and sometimes for bones and collagen. One small trial supports a testosterone rise; the physique and ageing uses rest on traditional claims and anecdote.

summary: Himalayan mineral resin sold for testosterone and vitality; one small trial supports a testosterone rise, and quality control is the open question.
note: Composition varies by source; raw resin may contain contaminants per general references, and most trials used purified proprietary extracts.
currentQuick:
Shilajit is a tar-like mountain exudate used for thousands of years in Ayurveda as a rejuvenating tonic. It is sold as a resin, capsule or gummy for testosterone, energy and recovery.
A small randomised trial in healthy men reported higher testosterone and DHEAS after 90 days of purified shilajit, and other trials have looked at bone and collagen markers. Evidence remains limited and mostly involves proprietary extracts.
How it works: It is made up mostly of humic substances such as fulvic acid plus minerals. Proposed antioxidant and hormonal effects come from lab and small human studies; its exact composition and origin are not fully characterised.
Risks and caveats: Purified products are described as generally well tolerated in small trials, while raw material may contain contaminants such as heavy metals according to general references. Content varies by source, and it is sold as a supplement.
deepLead:
Shilajit (also mumijo, moumiyo or mummiyo) is a sticky, dark, tar-like substance that seeps from rock layers in high mountain ranges such as the Himalayas, long used in Ayurvedic and other traditional medicine as a rejuvenator (rasayana) and adaptogen. It consists mainly of humic substances (a review puts them at more than 80 percent of its weight) together with minerals and plant and microbial metabolites.
It is sold as a resin, powder, capsule or gummy and marketed for testosterone, energy, recovery and vitality. A small randomised, placebo-controlled trial in healthy men aged 45 to 55 reported higher total testosterone, free testosterone and DHEAS after 90 days of purified shilajit. Other human trials have examined bone density in postmenopausal women, fracture repair, and a collagen biomarker, while a 2024 review of testosterone boosters named a purified shilajit extract in its findings.
Reviewers describe its chemical composition and origin as not fully established, and the human research is limited to small trials, many using proprietary purified extracts.

name: Cistanche

angle.text: Cistanche is a Chinese tonic herb that bodybuilding forums list as a testosterone and DHT booster, used for libido, strength and recovery, including after cycles. Human trials on these uses are essentially absent.

summary: A Chinese tonic herb that bodybuilding forums list as a test and DHT booster; human trials on those claims are essentially absent.
note: Small human trials exist for strength, cognition and fatigue; none found for testosterone or DHT.
currentQuick:
Cistanche is the dried stem of a parasitic desert plant used for centuries in traditional Chinese medicine as a kidney and vitality tonic. Extracts are sold as supplements.
In forums it is mentioned as a testosterone or DHT booster and as part of post-cycle herb stacks. The research available is mostly lab and animal work, plus a few small trials on strength, cognition and fatigue.
How it works: Its phenylethanoid glycosides such as echinacoside and acteoside show antioxidant and neuroprotective effects in cell and animal studies. How, or whether, this would change androgen levels in people has not been shown in trials found here.
Risks and caveats: Trials reported so far are small and short, and it is approved as a food ingredient in China. Long-term safety data in healthy men are limited, and wild C. deserticola is on CITES Appendix II.
deepLead:
Cistanche is a genus of parasitic desert plants whose fleshy stems, chiefly from Cistanche deserticola and Cistanche tubulosa, are used as a tonic in traditional Chinese medicine under the name Rou Cong Rong, sometimes called "desert ginseng" . Traditional uses include treating kidney deficiency, impotence, female infertility and constipation in older people .
In bodybuilding and testosterone-optimisation communities, Cistanche tubulosa extract is sold as a herbal supplement and is described by some users as a test booster or a DHT booster, often stacked with other herbs during post-cycle therapy . Laboratory and animal research has examined its phenylethanoid glycosides (echinacoside, acteoside) for antioxidant, neuroprotective, liver-protective and bone-related effects .
Human trials of Cistanche extracts are few and small. They have looked at muscle strength and recovery, locomotive function, cognition and fatigue . No published trial identified here has measured testosterone-raising or DHT-raising effects as a cosmetic or physique outcome.

name: Kisspeptin

angle.text: Kisspeptin-10 is a hypothalamic peptide that TRT users discuss as an hCG alternative to keep the testes active and to aid post-cycle recovery. Kisspeptin has been given to people in research and shown to raise LH; the TRT use has not been tested.

summary: A hypothalamic peptide that triggers LH release; forums pitch kisspeptin-10 as an hCG alternative, but no trial tests that use.
note: Not an approved drug; human trials are small academic studies, not in men on testosterone therapy.
currentQuick:
Kisspeptin is a natural signalling peptide that tells the hypothalamus to release GnRH, which drives LH and testosterone. Its fragment kisspeptin-10 is sold as a research peptide.
Testosterone-therapy forums discuss it as an alternative to hCG or gonadorelin for keeping testicular signalling going. Academic trials show it raises LH in volunteers, but none tests this forum use.
How it works: It binds KISS1R on GnRH neurons, increasing GnRH pulses and thereby LH and FSH from the pituitary. In men, LH stimulates testicular testosterone production.
Risks and caveats: It has no approved indication, and products are unregulated research chemicals. Long-term effects of repeated self-administration have not been established in the cited trials, and effects on appearance outcomes are untested.
deepLead:
Kisspeptins are a family of neuropeptides encoded by the KISS1 gene. They act on the receptor KISS1R (GPR54) on gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons in the hypothalamus, which makes them a key upstream signal for luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and, in men, testosterone . The shortest fully active fragment, kisspeptin-10, and the longer kisspeptin-54 have both been given to people in research settings .
In testosterone-therapy and bodybuilding forums, kisspeptin-10 is discussed as a way to keep the testes signalling during testosterone replacement or after a steroid cycle, as an alternative to hCG or gonadorelin . This is an off-label, non-approved use of a research peptide; no kisspeptin product is an approved medicine.
Human studies of kisspeptin are real but small and are conducted by academic endocrinology groups. They show it raises gonadotropins in healthy volunteers and some patients with reproductive disorders . No trial found here has tested it for muscle, physique or other appearance outcomes.

name: Gonadorelin

angle.text: Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH that TRT users take as a substitute for hCG to prevent testicular atrophy. It is established in fertility medicine and diagnostics; its use as an hCG substitute is untested, and forum posters disagree about its effectiveness.

summary: Synthetic GnRH that TRT forums use as an hCG substitute; established for fertility medicine, untested for that use.
note: Proven in pulsatile fertility therapy; no trial versus hCG in men on testosterone.
currentQuick:
Gonadorelin is lab-made GnRH, the brain signal that makes the pituitary release LH and FSH. Doctors have used it for diagnostic testing and, as pulsed infusions, to restore ovulation or fertility in people with GnRH deficiency.
On TRT forums it is used in place of hCG to keep the testes active. Users report mixed results, and no trial has compared the two in that setting.
How it works: It binds GnRH receptors on the pituitary, triggering LH and FSH release. Because it is cleared within minutes, its effects depend on how it is pulsed, and continuous exposure desensitises receptors.
Risks and caveats: Documented trials are in specialist reproductive settings. In TRT use, reports are anecdotal, some users describe persistent atrophy, and supply may come from clinics or compounding sources of varying regulation.
deepLead:
Gonadorelin is the synthetic form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the hypothalamic decapeptide that prompts the pituitary to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) . In medicine it has been used to test pituitary responsiveness and, delivered in pulses, to induce ovulation in women with hypothalamic amenorrhea .
In testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) and bodybuilding communities, gonadorelin is discussed as a substitute for hCG to keep the testes stimulated and avoid atrophy while on exogenous testosterone. Some clinics prescribe it for this purpose, and forum users report mixed experiences .
Published trials cover diagnostic and fertility uses in patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or amenorrhea . No trial found here has compared gonadorelin with hCG in men on testosterone therapy, and none has examined appearance outcomes.

name: Pregnenolone

angle.text: Users take pregnenolone because it is the precursor to testosterone, cortisol and DHEA, hoping to support hormone levels and, through them, muscle and leanness. Trials exist for mood and psychiatric uses; a testosterone or appearance effect from supplementing is untested.

summary: The body's master steroid precursor, sold as a supplement for hormone support; trials exist for psychiatric uses, none for testosterone or looks.
note: Downstream conversion varies by person; no trials in healthy men for hormone or appearance outcomes.
currentQuick:
Pregnenolone is made from cholesterol and sits at the start of the steroid pathway, leading to progesterone, cortisol, DHEA, testosterone and estrogens. It is also made in the brain.
On forums it is taken for hormone support, mood and libido, and discussed through the 'pregnenolone steal' idea. Controlled trials have been psychiatric, not about testosterone or appearance.
How it works: The body converts it enzymatically into other steroids, and it acts as a neurosteroid in the brain. Whether swallowed pregnenolone becomes testosterone in a useful way in healthy men has not been shown in the cited trials.
Risks and caveats: Because it feeds several hormone pathways, effects can be unpredictable, and a forum poster advises supervision. It is sold as a US supplement with limited regulatory evaluation; long-term data in healthy users are lacking.
deepLead:
Pregnenolone is a steroid made from cholesterol that serves as the biosynthetic precursor of other steroid hormones, including progesterone, cortisol, DHEA, testosterone and estrogens . It is produced in the adrenal glands, gonads and brain, and is also classed as a neurosteroid . It is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement in the United States.
In looksmaxxing and testosterone-optimisation circles it is discussed as a hormone-support supplement, often alongside DHEA, and in the concept of "pregnenolone steal", the idea that stress and stimulants divert pregnenolone away from sex-hormone production toward cortisol . Users report supplementing for mood, libido, anxiety and brain fog .
Controlled trials of oral pregnenolone have been conducted mainly in psychiatry, such as bipolar depression and schizophrenia . No trial found here has tested it for testosterone levels, physique or appearance outcomes.

name: Yohimbine

chain: Raises fat release from stubborn areas
angle.text: Cutters use yohimbine, often with caffeine and fasted cardio, to target stubborn fat and get leaner in the face and midsection. The alpha-2 rationale is based on mechanism and small studies in athletes; trials in men aimed at visible fat loss are limited.

summary: An alpha-2 blocker stimulant used in cutting stacks for stubborn fat; the fat-loss rationale is mostly untested in men and the side effects are real.
note: Raises heart rate and blood pressure; anxiety common. Legal status varies by country.
currentQuick:
Yohimbine comes from yohimbe bark and blocks alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which increases noradrenaline activity. It is a common ingredient in pre-workouts and fat burners.
Cutting forums use it for stubborn fat, often with caffeine and fasted cardio. The studies found here are small topical-fat trials and research uses of the drug as a stress probe; none shows oral fat loss in dieting men.
How it works: By blocking presynaptic alpha-2 receptors it raises norepinephrine release, which proponents say promotes lipolysis in fat depots that resist it. The effect is short-lived, with a half-life reported as under about an hour.
Risks and caveats: Documented adverse effects include anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate and gastrointestinal upset, with rare severe cases. It requires a prescription in some countries and is sold as a supplement in others.
deepLead:
Yohimbine is an indole alkaloid obtained from the bark of the African tree Pausinystalia yohimbe. It acts as a selective antagonist of alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which raises norepinephrine release and sympathetic activity . It has been used in folk medicine as an aphrodisiac, and prescription yohimbine hydrochloride has been studied for erectile dysfunction .
In bodybuilding and cutting circles it is promoted as a fat-loss supplement, particularly for "stubborn" fat and for use with fasted cardio. The reasoning is that alpha-2 receptors in some fat depots resist lipolysis and yohimbine blocks them . It is an ingredient in many pre-workout and fat-burner products .
Published evidence on fat loss is thin. A 1995 set of small trials tested topical yohimbine-containing preparations on women's thigh fat . Reviews of erectile dysfunction treatments and natural aphrodisiacs discuss it as a candidate . Known adverse effects include anxiety, raised blood pressure and heart rate, and gastrointestinal upset .

name: Synephrine

angle.text: Bitter-orange synephrine is used in fat burners and pre-workouts as an ephedra substitute to help users cut body fat. Small trials show more fat oxidation during exercise; long-term fat loss and visible body changes are unproven.

summary: Bitter-orange stimulant sold as the ephedra replacement; small trials show more fat oxidation during exercise, long-term fat loss unproven.
note: Cardiovascular concerns, especially stacked with caffeine or other stimulants.
currentQuick:
Synephrine is the main active amine of bitter orange extract, sold in fat burners and pre-workouts as an ephedra-free stimulant.
Small crossover trials found it increases fat oxidation during exercise. Evidence that it produces lasting fat loss is limited, and little forum discussion is dedicated to it.
How it works: It is a sympathomimetic amine thought to act mainly on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors with weak beta effects, which differs from ephedrine. Acute exercise trials measure higher fat oxidation rates after a dose.
Risks and caveats: Short controlled trials in healthy adults report good tolerance, while observational reports link bitter orange to blood-pressure and cardiovascular problems, mainly with stimulant stacks. Legal status is as a dietary supplement in the US.
deepLead:
Synephrine is a protoalkaloid of the phenethylamine class found chiefly in the immature fruit of the bitter orange, Citrus aurantium. Its main natural form is p-synephrine . It is a sympathomimetic compound, and extracts are sold in weight-loss and pre-workout supplements, often as a replacement for ephedra .
The supplement industry markets it for appetite suppression, fat loss and energy. Grokipedia describes clinical evidence for these effects as modest and often involving combination with caffeine . A series of small randomized crossover trials in exercising adults reported that acute p-synephrine ingestion raised the rate of fat oxidation during exercise . Whether this translates into long-term fat loss has not been established in the trials cited here.
Safety discussion centres on cardiovascular effects, particularly when bitter orange is combined with caffeine or other stimulants . Community discussion specific to synephrine is sparse; it appears mostly as an ingredient in energy and fat-burner products.

name: Liothyronine (T3)

chain: Faster fat loss on a cut
angle.text: Some cutters use T3, a prescription thyroid hormone, off-label to speed fat loss and reduce puffiness around the eyes and face. It is approved for hypothyroidism; use for appearance is off-label and not supported by trials, and the label warns against it for weight loss.

summary: The active thyroid hormone, a real hypothyroidism drug that cutters misuse for fat loss; the FDA label carries a boxed warning against that.
note: Boxed warning: not for obesity or weight loss; large doses in euthyroid patients may be life-threatening.
currentQuick:
Liothyronine is lab-made T3, the active thyroid hormone, prescribed for hypothyroidism and in some thyroid cancer care. Some physique communities use it off-label for fat loss, and one looksmax.org thread claims it reduces eye puffiness.
Trials cover thyroid, depression and heart conditions, not fat loss or looks in healthy people.
How it works: T3 enters cells and binds thyroid receptors in the nucleus, changing gene transcription and raising the body's metabolic activity. In people with normal thyroid function, supplemental hormone suppresses their own thyroid output.
Risks and caveats: The label's boxed warning says it should not be used for obesity or weight loss and that large doses may be life-threatening. Overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms, heart rhythm problems and bone effects. It is prescription-only in the US.
deepLead:
Liothyronine is the synthetic form of triiodothyronine (T3), the active thyroid hormone, sold in the United States as Cytomel and as generics. It is approved to treat hypothyroidism, to suppress thyroid-stimulating hormone as an adjunct in thyroid cancer care, and in thyroid suppression testing .
In bodybuilding and cutting culture, T3 has been used off-label by people without thyroid disease to raise metabolic rate and lose fat. A looksmax.org thread also describes a user who credits T3 pills with reducing puffiness around the eyes . The FDA label carries a boxed warning that thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss, stating that in euthyroid patients doses within the usual replacement range are ineffective for weight reduction and that larger doses may produce serious or life-threatening toxicity .
Controlled trials of liothyronine concern hypothyroidism, depression augmentation, heart disease and other medical conditions . No trial found here tests it for fat loss or appearance in healthy people.

name: Hydroxyapatite (toothpaste)

angle.text: Users switch to hydroxyapatite toothpaste as a fluoride-free way to protect enamel and keep teeth smooth and bright. One 18-month adult trial matched fluoride for cavity prevention; whitening claims have thin evidence.

summary: A fluoride-free remineralising toothpaste built on enamel's own mineral; one 18-month adult trial matched fluoride for caries, whitening claims are thin.
note: Trials mostly compare with fluoride; evidence for whitening on its own was not found.
currentQuick:
Hydroxyapatite toothpaste uses the same mineral that makes up tooth enamel, in tiny particles, as a fluoride-free way to protect and remineralise teeth.
An 18-month adult trial found it not inferior to fluoride at preventing new cavities, and a child trial and small sensitivity trials have also been positive. Evidence that it whitens teeth by itself was not found.
How it works: Particles are meant to deposit on enamel and fill microscopic defects in demineralised areas, supported by saliva's calcium and phosphate. In bleaching trials it reduced sensitivity when added to peroxide.
Risks and caveats: Trials report no safety concerns, and the main safety debate in the field concerns fluoride rather than hydroxyapatite. Long-term, large-scale data are still limited.
deepLead:
Hydroxyapatite toothpaste contains synthetic hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral that is also the main mineral of tooth enamel, in micro- or nano-sized crystals. It is marketed as a fluoride-free alternative for protecting and remineralising enamel . Review authors describe how the particles deposit on and restore demineralised enamel surfaces, and they are being explored as an anti-caries agent without fluoride .
Interest in it connects to appearance through tooth health, enamel erosion, sensitivity and whitening: trials have examined it for dentin hypersensitivity, for reducing sensitivity during bleaching, and for erosive enamel lesions .
An 18-month randomized trial in adults found a fluoride-free hydroxyapatite toothpaste not inferior to a 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste for preventing new caries , and a 24-month trial in children reported results favouring hydroxyapatite-fluoride toothpastes on active enamel lesions . Fluoride remains the long-established standard in caries prevention .

name: Hyaluronic acid filler

angle.text: HA filler is injected to add volume and reshape the lips, cheekbones, chin, jawline and under-eye area, so the change in facial contour is visible right after treatment. Its volume effect is well studied, and it can be dissolved with an enzyme if users want to reverse it.

summary: The standard injectable filler: reversible gel for lips, cheeks and folds, well studied for volume, rare but serious vascular risks.
note: Rare vascular occlusion can cause tissue loss or permanent vision loss; provider skill matters.
currentQuick:
Hyaluronic acid fillers are injectable gels used to add volume and smooth folds in the lips, cheeks and lines around the mouth. They are the most widely used type of dermal filler, and randomized trials and meta-analyses support their effect on volume and wrinkles.
Results are temporary, commonly lasting around six months or longer depending on product and area, and the gel can be dissolved with an enzyme if the result is unwanted.
How it works: The gel physically fills space and binds water, and some studies report that it also prompts nearby skin cells to make new collagen.
Risks and caveats: Most side effects are short-lived swelling, redness and bruising. Rare but serious complications include blocked blood vessels causing tissue death and, in the worst cases, permanent vision loss; guidelines describe emergency treatment with hyaluronidase. In the US fillers are regulated as medical devices and injected by licensed providers.
deepLead:
Hyaluronic acid (HA) fillers are injectable gels, most often based on cross-linked hyaluronic acid, placed under the skin to restore volume, soften folds and wrinkles, and reshape areas such as the lips, cheeks and nasolabial folds. Hyaluronic acid is a naturally occurring component of skin, and reviews describe HA gels as the most commonly used dermal filler . Well-known product lines include Juvederm and Restylane.
Clinicians describe HA fillers as temporary and reversible: the gel can be dissolved with the enzyme hyaluronidase, and the effect may last longer than the physical persistence of the gel because of possible collagen stimulation . Randomized trials and systematic reviews report that most side effects are short-lived injection-site reactions such as swelling and bruising, while rare complications, including vascular occlusion and vision loss, can be serious and in some cases permanent .
In looksmaxxing discussions the procedure appears mainly as a non-surgical option for lips, cheeks, chin and under-eye hollows, usually discussed alongside surgery and fat grafting. The published evidence on its effect on facial attractiveness specifically is limited to a small number of studies, while evidence for volume and wrinkle correction is more extensive .

name: Glutathione (IV)

angle.text: Glutathione drips are promoted in some clinics for skin lightening and a more even tone, based on lab findings about melanin production. Reviews find limited clinical evidence for this appearance use.

summary: Injected antioxidant sold as a skin-whitening drip; reviews find no proof it works for this and flag anaphylaxis and liver-toxicity risks.
note: Reviews link IV use for lightening to serious adverse events; the Philippine FDA has acted on reports.
currentQuick:
IV glutathione is the injected form of a natural antioxidant, offered in some clinics as a way to lighten skin tone. Lab studies show glutathione can interfere with melanin production, which is the basis for the claim.
Dermatology reviews report that no rigorous trials establish that the intravenous route lightens skin, and that standard dosing does not exist. Oral and topical forms have some small studies with variable results.
How it works: Glutathione is proposed to inhibit tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and to shift pigment production toward a lighter type.
Risks and caveats: Reviews associate IV use for lightening with anaphylaxis and liver toxicity concerns, and one regulator, the Philippine FDA, has acted on adverse-effect reports. A 2018 review did not recommend the IV route for skin lightening. Use for cosmetic lightening is off-label.
deepLead:
Glutathione is a small antioxidant tripeptide that cells make naturally; intravenous (IV) glutathione is the injected form that is promoted in some countries and cosmetic clinics as a systemic skin-lightening treatment . Proponents of the practice point to laboratory findings that glutathione can inhibit the enzyme tyrosinase and shift melanin production from the darker eumelanin toward the lighter pheomelanin .
Dermatology reviews report that there is a gap between the popularity of IV glutathione for skin lightening and the evidence behind it. A 2016 review stated that no evidence proves the efficacy of IV injections for this purpose and noted that adverse effects led the Philippine Food and Drug Administration to take regulatory action . A 2018 review of systemic lightening treatments did not suggest IV glutathione because of the risk of adverse events , and a 2025 narrative review linked it to anaphylaxis and liver toxicity concerns, with no standardized dosing .

name: Eye massage device

angle.text: Users apply warming or vibrating eye massagers hoping to reduce under-eye puffiness and dark circles. Studies have looked at dry-eye comfort; puffiness and dark circles have not been tested.

summary: Warming or vibrating under-eye massager; studied for dry-eye comfort, but no trial has tested puffiness or dark circles.
note: Published trials examine dry eye and blood flow, not under-eye appearance.
currentQuick:
Eye massage devices apply vibration, pulsing pressure or warmth around the eyes. They are marketed for puffiness and dark circles, among other uses.
The human studies that exist look at other outcomes, such as dry eye symptoms and eye blood flow. No trial found has tested whether these gadgets change under-eye appearance.
How it works: The devices apply gentle mechanical stimulation and often heat to the periorbital area; proposed benefits relate to circulation and relaxation.
Risks and caveats: No device-specific safety problems appear in the sources; a small dry-eye trial tracked eye redness and eye pressure as safety measures. General caution applies to pressure near the eye.
deepLead:
An eye massage device is a handheld or wearable gadget that applies gentle vibration, pulsing, pressure or warmth to the skin around the eyes. It is marketed in the beauty and wellness sector for relieving puffiness and dark circles, and in a separate medical and wellness context for eye comfort, with products such as the Foreo Iris named among its examples.
Published human research on such devices concerns other outcomes: a small crossover trial of a heating and vibrating eye mask for dry eye, a trial of periocular massage on ocular blood flow and visual acuity, and case reports of eye massagers used as a distraction in dental care . No published trial located in the sources has tested whether an eye massage device reduces under-eye puffiness or dark circles.

name: Microneedle stamp

angle.text: Looksmaxxers press derma stamps into the skin to smooth acne scars and texture and to try to thicken eyebrows or beard areas. Evidence comes from research on microneedling in general and small case series; stamp-specific trials are few.

summary: Press-in needle stamp for scars, brows and texture; little stamp-specific research, mostly small case series.
note: Needle devices carry infection risk if not sterile; no controlled trials for brows or beards.
currentQuick:
A microneedle stamp is a small handheld tool with a block of short needles that is pressed into the skin. It is a form of microneedling, used in clinics and at home for scars, skin texture and sometimes eyebrow or beard areas.
Research specific to stamps is thin: mostly small case series and a few trials, with no controlled trials found for brows, beards or acne scars.
How it works: The needles make tiny punctures that are proposed to trigger wound healing and collagen production and to help topical products enter the skin.
Risks and caveats: Any skin-puncturing device can cause irritation or infection if not kept sterile; health authorities have reported infections linked to non-clinical microneedling facials involving blood products. Evidence for appearance benefits is limited.
deepLead:
A microneedle stamp, also called a derma stamp or microneedle stamping device, is a handheld tool with a flat head of short needles that is pressed vertically into the skin. It is a variant of microneedling, the practice of repeatedly puncturing the skin with fine needles, which is used for scars and skin texture and is discussed on forums for eyebrow and hair areas .
Published research specific to stamps is sparse. A review of ten years of Korean microneedle-therapy literature found only 7 animal studies, 2 clinical trials and 10 case studies, mostly on skin and hair . Evidence for a stamp-delivered growth-factor treatment is limited to a 30-woman case series . Wikipedia notes that research on microneedling combined with other agents is ongoing and that cases of infection have followed non-clinical microneedling facials .

name: Microneedling pen (electric)

angle.text: Electric microneedling pens are used for acne scars, texture, stretch marks and thinning hair, and are a staple of skin routines in looksmaxxing forums. Small trials support benefits for scars and texture; claims about depth and generic versus branded pens rest largely on user reports.

summary: Motorised needle pen for collagen induction; decent small-trial support for scars and texture, but rare reactions and depth/hygiene issues at home.
note: Rare granulomatous reactions reported, mostly with motorized pens and topical vitamin C.
currentQuick:
An electric microneedling pen rapidly punctures the skin with fine disposable needles to trigger repair. It is used for acne scars, texture, stretch marks and sometimes hair or pigment problems, and is a staple of looksmax skincare talk.
Small randomized studies report improvement in acne scars, often better when combined with peels or other agents, but many trials are small and from single centres, and long-term data are limited.
How it works: The needles create micro-injuries that start wound healing, release growth factors and stimulate collagen and elastin production, and the channels may help topical products penetrate.
Risks and caveats: A systematic review described microneedling as relatively safe overall. Rare granulomatous reactions have been reported, with motorized pens and topical vitamin C implicated in most cases. Forum discussions of deep home settings are personal reports rather than clinical guidance.
deepLead:
An electric microneedling pen is a motorised handheld device that drives a cartridge of fine needles rapidly up and down into the skin to create controlled micro-injuries. It is used for acne scars, skin texture, stretch marks, pigmentation disorders and hair thinning, and is a staple of skin and scar discussion in looksmaxxing forums; the Dermapen is the best-known branded example .
Dermatology research on microneedling, including pen devices, consists largely of small trials, many from single centres, that compare it with peels or other treatments or use it to deliver topical products and platelet-rich plasma. A systematic review of 51 articles and 1,029 patients described microneedling as a relatively safe procedure . Rare but notable adverse reactions have been reported, including granulomatous reactions in which motorized pens and topical vitamin C application were implicated in most published cases .
